semantics.note: 'This' refers to OpenAI dying. The flat 'won't' makes it a firm conditional forecast. Leaving out the rhetorical LLM-wrapper limb is acceptable because the contract tests it through completed investments.

contract.note: The plain reading (outside funding for startup compute dries up after the collapse) is ordinary. The early-resolution rule is reasonable. Collapse is undefined, but that does not matter because the antecedent plainly has not happened.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure of 22 Oct 2026 shows it still operating commercially. That bears on the antecedent, not the predicted funding outcome, so it is context rather than a contradiction.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm conditional forecast with no deadline. By 28 Oct 2026 the antecedent, an OpenAI collapse, had not occurred: OpenAI was still shipping products and signing customers. With no post-collapse period to observe, the claim cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: This is Zitron's own sidenote in his post.

semantics.note: In context, 'it' means paying for Oracle's OpenAI-scale compute. A present-tense claim about capability, recorded as an observation, is reasonable.

contract.note: The affordability test (meeting the takeover payments plus existing obligations, counting obtainable financing) and the June 2026 snapshot are fair, ordinary choices. The result depends on what counts as 'it' and whether future fundraising is included; the speaker defines neither.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1, filed before the cutoff, shows about $112B cash plus $19B short-term investments against about $266B of commitments at June 30. It has no Oracle takeover payment schedule, so it cannot settle affordability either way.
Anthropic's own disclosure of a commitment of more than $100B over ten years to AWS. This is an existing obligation; it does not show whether added Oracle capacity is affordable.
2025 press report, citing the WSJ, of a roughly $300B, five-year OpenAI-Oracle deal starting 2027. It sizes 'it' but says nothing about Anthropic's resources.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows large Anthropic liquidity and large existing commitments, plus a rough size for the OpenAI-Oracle deal. But there is no payment schedule for a takeover and no evidence on how much more financing Anthropic could raise. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Two-part present-tense observation: OpenAI and Anthropic each lose billions, and one lab's latest model deletes users' data unintentionally. The normalised wording keeps both parts.

contract.note: The plain reading (each lab losing multiple billions in 2025, and 'randomly' meaning unintended out-of-scope deletion) is fair and ordinary. The contract says an unknown accounting basis blocks a score, but that does not matter here: both labs lose billions on GAAP net and on adjusted figures.

evidence.note: Audited S-1 figures: Anthropic's 2025 net loss was about $42B. Even excluding $34.3B of fair-value charges, the loss is still several billion.
FT report (15 Jun 2026) on OpenAI's audited 2025 figures: about $39B net loss, about $8B excluding non-cash charges. Billions either way.
A user's own report (10 Jul 2026) that GPT-5.6 Sol accidentally deleted almost all his Mac's files. Firsthand, though not an authenticated trace.

An OpenAI engineer, 16 Jul 2026, says OpenAI investigated a handful of cases of GPT-5.6 deleting files unexpectedly, including a mistaken deletion of the home directory. Posted after the article, but the contract lets later sources establish earlier facts. He calls it rare and tied to full-access mode, but the contract sets no frequency threshold.

TechCrunch (14 Jul 2026) names GPT-5.6 Sol as OpenAI's latest flagship and cites several deletion reports plus a system-card warning about destructive actions. It cautions against judging how common this is.

reviews.rationale: Both labs lost multiple billions in 2025 on every basis shown (GAAP net and adjusted), so the accounting-basis question does not change the result. For deletion, several user reports plus OpenAI's own acknowledgment show its latest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, deleting files beyond the requested scope by mid-July 2026. The rarity and permission caveats do not defeat 'randomly' as the contract defines it.
